name: Fapfap
description: Fapfap, known as Agram in Niger and Mali, is a simple yet strategic last-trick-only game from West Africa. Players compete to win the final trick after five rounds of play, with the unusual twist that winning earlier tricks can be a disadvantage as it forces you to lead and cede control. A stripped 35-card deck is used, with unique ranking and the removal of the Ace of Spades.

history.origins: Originating in the Sahel region of West Africa, Fapfap evolved from European trick-taking games introduced during the colonial era. The game is known by different names across the region: Agram in Niger and Mali, Sink-Sink in parts of Niger, and Fapfap in Cameroon. It is closely related to Sparrow in Ghana.
timeline: Colonial Era: European trick-taking mechanics adapted by West African populations with regional card removals and rules modifications.
20th Century: Established as a staple social game throughout the Sahel, played in cafes and street gatherings.
Modern Era: Popular in Cameroon and across West Africa; remains largely unknown in Western card gaming circles.
history.cultural: Played as a fast-paced social game, often for small monetary stakes or social prestige. Traditionally played in informal social settings and commercial gatherings.
history.evolution: Regional variants developed unique deck compositions and scoring systems. The Cameroon version (Fapfap) emphasizes the final trick with multiplier bonuses for winning with low cards (3s, 4s).

setup.deck: 35-card stripped deck. Take a standard 52-card deck and remove: all Kings, all Queens, all Jacks, all 2s, and the Ace of Spades (The Chief). Remaining deck: Ace (except Spades), 3-10 of all suits.
setup.dealing: Dealer (rotates clockwise) shuffles; right-hand player cuts. Dealer distributes 5 or 6 cards to each player (depending on regional variant) in two batches. Cameroon: 6 cards (3, then 3). Niger: 5 cards (3, then 2).
setup.equipment: Deck and chips/stakes for optional scoring variant.

rules.objective: Win the final (5th or 6th) trick. Winning earlier tricks may be disadvantageous as the trick winner must lead the next trick.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Starting Play**: The player to the dealer's right leads the first trick with any card. 2. **Following Suit**: Players must follow the suit of the led card if able. If unable, any card may be played. 3. **Winning a Trick**: The highest card of the led suit wins the trick. No trump suit exists. 4. **Next Lead**: The winner of the trick leads the next trick with any card. 5. **Final Trick**: After 5 or 6 tricks (depending on variant), the winner of the last trick wins the game. 6. **Round Completion**: After each complete game, the deal passes to the next player clockwise.
keyRules: Card rank order (high to low): Ace, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 (except Spades: 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 only; no Ace of Spades).
Must follow suit if able; otherwise, play any card.
Only the final trick matters; earlier trick wins are often strategic disadvantages.
No trump suit in standard play.
Trick winner leads the next trick, forcing them to potentially give away control.

strategy.basic: Avoid winning early tricks if possible. Sluff (discard) low-to-mid range cards early to preserve high cards (Aces, 10s) for the final trick. If you must win, do so with the lowest possible card.
strategy.intermediate: The 3 Strategy: The 3 is the weakest card but carries a multiplier bonus in Cameroon variant. Winning the final trick with a 3 is more valuable than with higher cards because of the stake multiplier, though it requires precise control of previous tricks.
strategy.advanced: Suit Tracking: Memorize which high cards (particularly Aces and 10s) have been played in each suit. Position yourself to lead the final trick with a card that others cannot beat with their remaining cards. Force opponents into wasteful high-card plays early by leading their strong suits.
tips: Never waste an Ace or 10 winning an early trick unless absolutely necessary.
If you win the 4th or 5th trick with a low card, you control the lead for the final trick and can play your strongest card.
Count remaining players' likely hand strength: after 4 tricks, estimate what each opponent still holds.
In Cameroon stakes variant, taking two consecutive tricks (especially the last two) with 3's is the ultimate combo.

scoring.description: Winner is determined by final trick victory. Optional chip-based scoring modifies stakes based on the winning card rank.
scoring.winCondition: First player to win the final (5th or 6th) trick wins the round.

synthesis.shortDescription: A West African trick-taking game where only the final trick determines the winner, inverting traditional trick-taking strategy.
